This word means 'to descend' and indicates a voluntary action of God to intervene in the situation of the oppressed. It reveals God's divine will to act on behalf of His people, showing that God does not remain distant from human suffering. Spiritually, this reinforces the idea that God is close to those who suffer and that He moves to bring deliverance.

This term means 'to send' and is often used to designate a mission or divine calling. In this verse, it emphasizes that God chooses Moses as an instrument of His deliverance. This highlights the fact that God uses people to accomplish His purposes and that every believer may be called to play a role in the divine plan.

34.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around 1446 B.C., a period of great suffering for God's people.
34.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech, which recalls the history of Israel and how God intervened to save His people. It emphasizes God's faithfulness in the face of oppression.
34.culture: In Hebrew culture, suffering and oppression are often seen as opportunities for God to demonstrate His power and mercy. Deliverance is a central theme of Israelite identity.
34.interpretation: This verse shows that God is attentive to the sufferings of His people and that He is ready to act to deliver them. It also reminds us that God calls individuals to be His instruments of salvation in the world.
34.commentaire: This passage teaches us that God sees and hears our sufferings. Like Moses, we are called to respond to God's call to act on behalf of the oppressed. This encourages us to be sensitive to the needs of others and to seek to be instruments of divine deliverance in our world.

mots.sens: The name 'Moses' means 'drawn out of the waters.' It evokes the idea of deliverance and divine protection, as Moses was saved from the waters of the Nile to become the liberator of Israel. This name is loaded with theological significance, highlighting Moses' role as God's instrument to free His people from slavery.

This term means 'leader' or 'pioneer.' It designates one who opens the way or leads a group. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes Moses' role as a spiritual guide and leader, chosen by God to lead His people to freedom and the promised land.

The word 'angel' means 'messenger.' In this verse, it refers to the angel of God who communicates with Moses in the burning bush. This shows that God uses messengers to convey His will and underscores the importance of divine intervention in the history of salvation.

This term means 'redemption' or 'liberation.' It evokes the idea of saving someone from a situation of oppression. In this context, it highlights Moses' role as a liberator sent by God, thus foreshadowing the ultimate redemption that Christ brings to humanity.

35.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, a time when the Christian community faced persecutions and tensions with traditional Judaism.
35.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech, which recalls the history of Israel and emphasizes the rejection of Moses by his own people, while affirming that it is God who chose him to be their liberator.
35.culture: In Jewish culture, the rejection of a divinely chosen leader is a recurring theme, illustrating the people's resistance to God's will. This rejection also reflects distrust towards established authorities.
35.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God often chooses people whom the world rejects to accomplish His purposes. Moses, though renounced, is a symbol of God's faithfulness to His promises and His ability to use imperfect instruments for His glory.
35.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of recognizing and accepting the leaders that God places in our path, even if they are rejected by others. It encourages us to trust in divine guidance, even in times of doubt and resistance, for God has a plan of redemption for each of us.

mots.sens: This term means 'miracles' or 'wonders.' It evokes divine actions that surpass human understanding and testify to God's power. In the context of the Exodus, these miracles are signs of divine intervention, strengthening the faith of the people and revealing God's sovereignty over the forces of nature. Theologically, this underscores that God is capable of delivering His people from all oppression.

The word 'signs' designates events or actions that carry spiritual significance. In the account of the Exodus, these signs serve to confirm Moses' mission and demonstrate God's power against the Egyptian idols. This reminds us that God uses signs to guide and encourage His people in their walk of faith.

This term means 'desert' or 'arid place.' It represents not only a physically difficult environment but also a period of trial and purification for the people of Israel. Spiritually, the desert is often a place of encounter with God, where one learns to depend entirely on Him. This underscores the importance of faith in times of uncertainty.

The word 'exodus' means 'exit' or 'departure.' It evokes the deliverance of the people of Israel from slavery in Egypt, symbolizing the spiritual liberation that God offers to all believers. Theologically, the exodus is a foreshadowing of redemption through Christ, who frees us from sin and death.

36.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the first century AD, when the early Church was developing and the apostles were testifying to God's power through the history of Israel.
36.passage: This passage is part of Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, who recalls the history of the people of Israel and God's faithfulness to His people, even in times of opposition.
36.culture: In Jewish culture, the accounts of the liberation from Egypt are central and are celebrated during Passover, recalling God's power and His commitment to His people.
36.interpretation: This verse highlights God's power in delivering His people, showing that He is capable of performing miracles for those who trust Him. It also reminds us that even in difficult times, God guides and protects His people.
36.commentaire: This passage encourages us to recognize God's power in our own lives. Just as God delivered Israel from slavery, He offers us spiritual deliverance through Christ. By relying on Him, we can navigate our personal deserts with faith, knowing that He is always by our side.

mots.sens: The word 'prophet' designates a spokesperson for God, someone who communicates divine will. It comes from the root 'phēmi,' which means 'to say' or 'to speak,' and implies a direct relationship with God. In this verse, Moses announces the coming of a prophet like him, which underscores the importance of divine revelation through intermediaries chosen by God.

The term 'brother' evokes a relationship of closeness and solidarity. In the biblical context, it can refer not only to blood ties but also to spiritual bonds among the members of God's people. This emphasizes that the coming prophet will be from the same people, reinforcing the idea of continuity in God's plan for His people.

The verb 'to raise up' means 'to elevate' or 'to bring forth.' It implies a divine action where God takes the initiative to send a messenger. This reveals God's sovereignty in history and His commitment to guide His people through inspired leaders.

37.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the first century, when the early Christians sought to understand their faith in light of the Hebrew Scriptures and the teachings of Jesus Christ.
37.passage: Acts 7 recounts Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he traces the history of Israel and highlights the people's rebellion against God's messengers, culminating in the announcement of Jesus' coming as the promised prophet.
37.culture: In Jewish culture, prophecy was a central element of faith, and the expectation of a prophet like Moses was deeply rooted in the collective imagination. The Jews hoped for a Messiah who would restore their nation and their relationship with God.
37.interpretation: This verse is a prophetic announcement that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, regarded as the prophet par excellence. It highlights the continuity between Moses and Jesus, reminding believers that God continues to speak through His messengers.
37.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God is faithful to His promises and raises up leaders to guide His people. As Christians, we are called to listen to the voice of Christ, the announced prophet, and to follow His teachings. This also invites us to be spokespersons for God in our own context, sharing His message of love and redemption.

mots.sens: This term means 'words' or 'oracles'. It is derived from 'λόγος' (logos), which refers to reason or divine speech. In this context, 'living oracles' refers to the divine instructions given by God, emphasizing their dynamic and vital nature for the people. This underscores the importance of divine revelation in the lives of believers, who are called to receive and transmit these truths.

This word means 'angel' or 'messenger'. It is used to designate spiritual beings sent by God to communicate His will. In this verse, the angel speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai represents the divine mediation between God and humanity, highlighting the importance of divine intervention in the process of revelation.

This term means 'father' and refers here to the ancestors of Israel. It evokes the historical and spiritual connection between generations of believers. By mentioning the fathers, the verse emphasizes the continuity of divine revelation throughout history and the importance of passing on the faith from one generation to the next.

38.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the 1st century, during the early days of the Christian Church, as the apostles preached the Gospel in a world dominated by paganism and Judaism. The Christian community sought to establish its identity and legitimacy in the face of Jewish traditions.
38.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recounts the history of Israel to demonstrate that God has always been active in revealing and guiding His people. It highlights Moses' role as an intermediary between God and the Israelites.
38.culture: In Jewish culture, the tradition of the ancestors and the transmission of divine teachings were of paramount importance. The oracles received by Moses were considered sacred instructions, essential for the life of the people of Israel.
38.interpretation: This verse highlights the continuity of divine revelation throughout history, showing that Moses received living oracles to pass on to the people. It also emphasizes Moses' central role as a mediator between God and Israel, a figure foreshadowing Christ, who is the ultimate mediator of the new covenant.
38.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of receiving and transmitting the word of God in our daily lives. As believers, we are called to be messengers of these living oracles, living according to divine instructions and sharing the truth of the Gospel with those around us. Like Moses, we have the responsibility to carry the light of God in our generation.

mots.sens: This term means 'to disobey' or 'not to submit'. It evokes an attitude of rebellion or refusal towards authority. In the context of this verse, it highlights the resistance of the ancestors of Israel to follow divine instructions, shedding light on their inclination to turn away from God. Spiritually, this reminds us that disobedience to God can lead to disastrous consequences.

This word means 'to turn' or 'to return'. In this verse, it illustrates the change of direction of the hearts of the ancestors of Israel towards Egypt, symbolizing their desire to return to a life of material comfort rather than faithfulness to God. This highlights the human tendency to seek earthly solutions instead of relying on divine providence.

The term 'heart' in this context refers not only to the physical organ but also to the source of thoughts, emotions, and decisions. It represents the center of human will. The heart's attachment to Egypt symbolizes a devotion to values and systems that oppose God's will, emphasizing the importance of keeping our hearts centered on Him.

Egypt, in the Bible, is often a symbol of oppression, idolatry, and disobedience to God. In this verse, the return to Egypt represents a desire to revert to practices and beliefs that oppose the worship of the God of Israel. This reminds us that the world can be alluring, but it is essential to remain faithful to our divine calling.

39.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the people of Israel, at the time when they were on their way to the Promised Land, after their exodus from Egypt. It is a transitional period marked by internal struggles and spiritual challenges.
39.passage: Acts 7 recounts Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he traces the history of Israel to illustrate their rejection of God and His messengers. This verse highlights the refusal of the ancestors to listen to Moses, which led to their wandering.
39.culture: The Israelite culture of the time valued obedience to God and faithfulness to His promises. However, the influence of Egypt, a symbol of comfort and security, created a temptation to return to idolatrous practices and lifestyles contrary to divine will.
39.interpretation: This verse highlights the human tendency to disobey God and turn away from His ways. The heart turned towards Egypt represents a quest for security and material comfort at the expense of spiritual faithfulness. This challenges us regarding our own tendency to seek solutions in the world instead of trusting God.
39.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of faithfulness to God, even in the face of worldly temptations. Like the ancestors of Israel, we can be seduced by promises of material security, but it is crucial to keep our hearts turned towards God. We must be vigilant in our obedience and commitment to Him, for therein lies our true freedom and peace.

mots.sens: This word means 'god' and refers to a deity, often used to designate the supreme God in the Bible. In this context, it underscores the search for a tangible representation of the divine, reflecting a deep human need for spiritual connection. The Israelites' demand for 'gods' reveals their inability to trust in the invisible and divine authority, highlighting the human tendency to create idols.

This term means 'to lead' or 'to guide'. It evokes the idea of direction and leadership, essential in the context of the exodus from Egypt. The Israelites, by asking for gods that 'walk before them', express their need for visible and tangible direction, underscoring their lack of faith in the divine guidance of Moses.

Moses is a central figure in the Old Testament, representing the law and deliverance. In this verse, his absence raises concerns among the people, revealing their spiritual fragility. Moses symbolizes the link between God and Israel, and his distance provokes a crisis of faith that drives them to seek divine substitutes.

40.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, when the Israelites, recently freed from Egyptian slavery, wander in the desert. It is a transitional period marked by challenges of identity and faith.
40.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen recalls the history of Israel to illustrate their rebellion against God. This verse highlights the moment when the people, faced with Moses' absence, choose to turn away from God to create idols, revealing their lack of trust.
40.culture: In the cultural context of the time, surrounding peoples worshiped physical idols and visible gods. The Israelites, influenced by these practices, show an inclination to adopt forms of worship that are familiar to them, illustrating the struggle between faith in the invisible and the need for material security.
40.interpretation: This verse illustrates the human tendency to seek substitutes for God when faith is tested. The Israelites, faced with uncertainty, choose to create gods that can be seen and touched, revealing their inability to trust in divine promise and spiritual direction.
40.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of faith in times of uncertainty. When we face challenges, it is crucial not to give in to the temptation to create modern 'idols', whether material or spiritual. By remaining steadfast in our trust in God and His guidance, we can avoid falling into the trap of unbelief.

mots.sens: This word means 'living' or 'animated', deriving from 'ἐν' (in) and 'ψυχή' (soul). In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of giving life to a human work, in contrast to the life that God gives. This underscores the folly of idolatry, where man creates a god in his own image, ignoring the living God who gave him life.

This term refers to the worship of idols, deriving from 'εἰδωλον' (idol) and 'λατρεία' (service or worship). It highlights the human tendency to turn away from God to worship human creations. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of keeping our worship centered on the true God, rather than on the works of our own hands.

This word means 'joy' or 'rejoicing', and is often associated with a state of deep happiness. In this verse, it emphasizes the fleeting satisfaction that the Israelites experience in worshiping their golden calf, contrasting with the lasting joy found in God. It invites us to reflect on the source of our joy and to direct it toward the Creator rather than toward idols.

41.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Old Testament, when the Israelites, after their exodus from Egypt, find themselves in the desert and begin to doubt God. It is a transitional period between slavery and the promise of the promised land.
41.passage: Acts 7 recounts Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recalls the history of Israel and its rebellions against God. This verse highlights the apostasy of the people who, in their impatience, turn to idolatry.
41.culture: In Israelite culture, the worship of material objects was a grave offense to God, who had revealed His uniqueness and sovereignty. The golden calf represents a tragic deviation from faith, influenced by the practices of surrounding nations.
41.interpretation: This verse illustrates the human tendency to create idols in response to anxiety and uncertainty. Spiritually, it warns us of how easily we can replace our worship of God with things we control, thus losing sight of our dependence on Him.
41.commentaire: The worship of the golden calf is a powerful reminder of our propensity to turn away from God to seek temporary solutions to our needs. This passage calls us to examine our own hearts and identify the 'idols' we may have raised in our lives. As believers, we must commit to worshiping the living God and seeking our joy in Him, rather than in the works of our hands.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to turn away' or 'to withdraw'. In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea that God, in response to Israel's idolatry, has turned away from His people. This underscores the seriousness of sin and the withdrawal of divine presence, resulting in spiritual consequences for those who choose to turn away from Him.

This term translates to 'worship' or 'adoration'. It refers to the idea of devoted service to God, but here it is used to describe the idolatrous worship of the host of heaven. This highlights Israel's betrayal, which, instead of worshiping the true God, engaged in idolatrous practices, which is an affront to the covenant relationship with God.

This word means 'sacrifice' or 'offering'. In the biblical context, sacrifices were expressions of devotion and repentance toward God. However, here it is used to remind that Israel offered sacrifices to idols, thus highlighting the irony of their situation: they thought they were honoring God while turning away from Him.

42.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the first century, when the early Christians, including Stephen, defended their faith in the face of Jewish opposition. It is a period marked by religious tensions and the transition between the old covenant and the new covenant in Christ.
42.passage: This passage is part of Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, who recalls the history of Israel to illustrate their disobedience to God. He uses references from the Old Testament to show how the people have constantly rejected God's messengers.
42.culture: At that time, idol worship was common in the Mediterranean world, and even among the Israelites, idolatrous practices had infiltrated. The reference to the host of heaven evokes pagan beliefs that were in direct opposition to Hebrew monotheism.
42.interpretation: This verse highlights the consequence of God's rejection by His people. By turning away from Him, God allowed them to be given over to their own desires, emphasizing the seriousness of idolatry and the danger of straying from divine truth.
42.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of remaining faithful to God and not being led astray by the distractions and idols of this world. It invites us to examine our own lives to see if we truly honor God or if we are turning away from Him through inappropriate practices. As believers, we must commit to worshiping the true God and living in accordance with His will.

mots.sens: Moloch is a pagan god associated with worship practices involving sacrifices, often of children. His name evokes extreme devotion and a tragic deviation from faith in God. In the biblical context, he represents idolatry and abandonment of divine ways, underscoring the seriousness of turning away from the Lord.

Remphan is a term that may refer to a celestial deity, often associated with the worship of the stars. The word evokes the idea of idolatry that diverts the people from the worship of the true God. Spiritually, it highlights the human tendency to seek substitutes for an authentic relationship with God.

The term skênê means 'tent' or 'tabernacle', symbolizing God's presence among His people. In this verse, it illustrates the contrast between divine presence and idolatry, emphasizing that the Israelites exchanged true worship for perverted practices. It reminds us of the importance of purity in our worship and devotion.

43.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, during the period of the early Church, where believers faced major persecutions and cultural challenges due to their faith in Christ.
43.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen defends his faith before the Sanhedrin, recalling the history of Israel and their rebellions against God. This verse highlights the idolatry of the people and their distance from true worship, leading to their exile.
43.culture: At that time, idol worship was common in the Greco-Roman world, and even among the Jews, there were pagan influences. This cultural context highlights the struggle between faithfulness to God and surrounding idolatrous practices.
43.interpretation: This verse illustrates the seriousness of idolatry and God's judgment on those who turn away from Him. It reminds believers that any form of worship that does not glorify the true God is doomed to failure and spiritual destruction.
43.commentaire: This passage exhorts us to examine our own lives and identify the 'idols' that may divert us from our authentic worship of God. It is essential to remain vigilant and cultivate a personal relationship with Christ, rejecting anything that might lead us away from Him. By focusing on the truth and purity of our worship, we can avoid the pitfalls of modern idolatry.

mots.sens: The word 'σκηνὴ' means 'tent' or 'tabernacle'. In the biblical context, it refers to the mobile structure that the Israelites used in the desert for worship. This term evokes not only a physical place but also the presence of God among His people, highlighting the intimate relationship between God and His people. Theologically, it foreshadows Christ, who came to dwell among us (John 1:14).

This term means 'testimony' or 'certificate'. It refers to the idea of bearing witness to divine truth, often through sacred objects or rituals. In the context of the tabernacle, it emphasizes the role of the tabernacle as a meeting place between God and humanity, where the testimony of the divine presence was manifested. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of our own testimony of faith in our daily lives.

This word means 'model' or 'example'. In the context of this verse, it refers to how Moses received precise instructions for building the tabernacle. This underscores the importance of following divine guidelines in worship and spiritual life. Theologically, it reminds us that God has a specific plan for our lives and that we are called to live according to His precepts.

44.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Old Testament, when the Israelites wandered in the desert after their exodus from Egypt, around 1446 B.C.
44.passage: Acts 7 presents Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recalls the history of Israel and God's faithfulness to His people, highlighting the tabernacle as a symbol of divine presence.
44.culture: In Israelite culture, the tabernacle was a central element of religious life, representing God's presence among His people and serving as a place of worship and sacrifice.
44.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of adhering to divine instructions in worship. The tabernacle, as a model, illustrates the necessity of a correct relationship with God, based on His revelation and commandments.
44.commentaire: The tabernacle of testimony is a powerful reminder of God's presence among His people. As Christians, we are called to live according to the model that Christ left us, seeking to honor God in our worship and daily lives. This verse encourages us to be faithful witnesses of God's truth in a world that needs His light.

mots.sens: This word refers to Jesus, whose name means 'Yahweh saves'. In the context of this verse, it refers to Joshua, which is the Hebrew form of the name. This parallel emphasizes that Joshua, as the leader of the people, foreshadows Jesus Christ, the true Savior who leads His people to the divine promise. The theological implication here is that just as Joshua led Israel into the promised land, Jesus leads us to our spiritual inheritance.

This term means 'father', and in this context, it refers to the ancestors of Israel. It evokes the idea of spiritual heritage and the promises of God passed down from generation to generation. It reminds us that God acts through family history and that the promises made to the ancestors are still valid for their descendants, thus highlighting God's faithfulness to His people.

This word means 'to chase' or 'to expel', and it refers to the action of God who drove out the nations before Israel. This indicates God's sovereignty over the nations and His active role in the history of Israel. Spiritually, it reminds us that God is capable of removing obstacles from our path to fulfill His promises, and that we must trust in His power.

This name refers to King David, a central figure in the history of Israel. David is often considered a man after God's own heart, and his reign represents a time of prosperity and closeness to God for the people. In the context of this verse, it underscores the continuity of God's work through the generations, and the promise of an eternal kingdom that will be fully realized in Christ.

45.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, when the emerging Christian Church faced opposition and persecution, and the apostles sought to establish the legitimacy of their faith by referring to the history of Israel.
45.passage: Acts 7 presents Stephen's speech, which traces the history of Israel to show how God has always been faithful to His people, even when they rejected His messengers. This verse highlights Israel's entry into the promised land under Joshua, marking a turning point in their history.
45.culture: Jewish culture deeply valued history and heritage, and ancestors were often referenced to remind of God's faithfulness. This historical and cultural context is essential for understanding the importance of the promise of the land and the role of Joshua.
45.interpretation: This verse illustrates the continuity of God's work throughout history, showing how He has guided His people from Egypt to the promised land. Spiritually, it reminds us that God is a God of covenant, who keeps His promises and guides His people through challenges.
45.commentaire: This passage encourages us to recognize God's faithfulness in our own lives. Just as He led Israel to the promised land, He guides us today in our walk of faith. We are called to trust His direction, even when we face obstacles, knowing that He has a plan for each of us.

mots.sens: This word means 'grace' and evokes unmerited favor and a free gift. In the context of this verse, it highlights God's kindness toward David, a man after God's own heart. Divine grace is a central theme in the relationship between God and humanity, illustrating how God chooses to bless those He loves, regardless of their merits.

This term translates to 'dwelling' or 'house', and it refers to a physical space where one lives, but also to the idea of God's presence among His people. David's request to build a temple for God underscores the desire to create a sacred place for worship and encounter with the divine, thus marking the importance of sanctifying places of worship in spiritual life.

This name refers to Jacob, a patriarch of Israel, and symbolizes the spiritual heritage and promises of God to His people. By mentioning 'the God of Jacob', the verse recalls the eternal covenant between God and Israel, and underscores the importance of the continuity of faith through generations.

46.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the Old Testament, at a time when Israel was seeking national and spiritual identity under the leadership of David, king of Israel.
46.passage: Acts 7:46 mentions David's desire to build a temple for God, a desire that illustrates his heart for the divine presence and the centrality of worship in Israel's life. This passage is part of a speech by Stephen, who recalls the history of God's people and the promises made to David.
46.culture: In Israelite culture, the construction of a temple was an act of devotion and a symbol of God's presence among His people. It also represented a way to gather the community around worship and adoration.
46.interpretation: God's grace toward David shows that even a sinful king can find favor with God, highlighting the importance of repentance and seeking divine will. David's request to raise a dwelling for God reveals a deep desire for closeness with the divine and to honor His greatness.
46.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God grants His grace to those who sincerely seek Him. Like David, we are called to desire a deeper relationship with God and to create spaces in our lives for His presence. Whether through prayer, worship, or community, we must commit to honoring God by seeking to establish a dwelling for Him in our hearts.

mots.sens: This term refers to the sanctuary or temple, particularly the most sacred part where the presence of God resided. It evokes the idea of separation between the sacred and the profane, and emphasizes the importance of holiness in worship. In the context of this verse, it symbolizes the fulfillment of God's divine promise to have a meeting place with His people.

Solomon, son of David, is known for his wisdom and wealth, as well as for building the first temple in Jerusalem. His name is often associated with peace and prosperity, representing the fulfillment of God's promises to Israel. This also highlights the role of royalty in the relationship between God and His people.

47.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the 1st century, at a time when the emerging Christian community was recalling the foundations of its faith, particularly the key figures of the Old Testament.
47.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen, in response to the accusations against him, recounts the history of Israel, highlighting God's faithfulness despite His people's unfaithfulness. This verse underscores the transition between the era of the patriarchs and the establishment of the temple by Solomon.
47.culture: The construction of the temple by Solomon is a central event in Jewish culture, symbolizing God's presence among His people and the ultimate place of worship. It also reflects the values of devotion and sacrifice that prevailed in Israelite society.
47.interpretation: The fact that Solomon built a house for God indicates the importance of a place of worship in the relationship between God and His people. It reminds believers that God desires to dwell among His people and that devotion and respect towards Him should manifest in places dedicated to prayer and worship.
47.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God has always wanted to establish a place where He could meet His people. As Christians, we are called to be living temples, carrying God's presence in our daily lives. This encourages us to create spaces in our lives for prayer and communion with God, while recognizing the importance of the Church as a community of believers.

mots.sens: This term refers to the sanctuary or temple, particularly the most sacred part where the presence of God resides. It evokes not only the idea of a physical place but also the notion of holiness and separation. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that the divine presence cannot be confined to human constructions, but transcends all material space.

This word means 'made by hand' and refers to anything created or manufactured by humans. It highlights the distinction between the divine and the human, shedding light on the limitations of human works compared to the greatness of God. This notion reminds us that God is not limited to material places of worship, but desires to dwell in the hearts of believers.

This term means 'prophet' and designates a person called by God to convey a divine message. In the context of this verse, it refers to God's voice throughout the ages, announcing the truth about His nature and presence. This underscores the importance of listening to the prophets, who remind believers of the reality of God's transcendence.

48.epoque: The verse is situated in the context of the 1st century, at a time when Christianity was emerging within a traditional Judaism facing challenges of identity and faith in the face of Greco-Roman culture.
48.passage: This passage is part of Stephen's speech, where he defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. He recalls the history of Israel and emphasizes that God is not limited to a place, but is present everywhere.
48.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the temple in Jerusalem was considered God's dwelling on earth. However, the understanding of divine presence was evolving with the advent of Christianity.
48.interpretation: This verse teaches us that God's presence cannot be confined to human structures. It reminds us that God is transcendent and that our relationship with Him does not depend on material places, but on our hearts and faith.
48.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our conception of God's presence. As believers, we must understand that God is not limited to a building, but desires to dwell within us. This pushes us to live our faith authentically, seeking a personal relationship with Him rather than relying on rituals or places of worship.

mots.sens: This word means 'heaven' and refers not only to the visible atmosphere but also to the spiritual realm where God resides. In this verse, it underscores God's sovereignty over the universe, affirming that even heaven, considered His throne, cannot contain His majesty. This reminds us that God transcends all creation and that His presence is not limited to a physical place.

The term 'earth' refers to the physical earth, but in a broader sense, it evokes the idea of creation and humanity. In this context, the earth is described as God's 'footstool,' indicating that even the foundations of our existence are under His authority. This reminds us that God is the creator of all and that nothing escapes Him.

This word means 'house' and can refer to both a physical building and a community of believers. In this verse, it questions humanity's ability to build a place worthy of God, highlighting the idea that God does not reside in structures made by human hands. This prompts us to reflect on the nature of our worship and our relationship with Him.

This term means 'place of rest' and evokes the idea of stability and presence. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that God is not seeking a physical place to rest, but rather a human heart open to His presence. This reminds us that our worship must be authentic and inward, rather than merely ritualistic.

49.epoque: This verse is situated in the context of the 1st century, where the early Christians faced religious and cultural tensions, particularly with Judaism and paganism.
49.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen, in response to accusations, recalls the history of Israel and emphasizes that God is not limited by human structures. This chapter highlights the transition from the old covenant to the new covenant in Christ.
49.culture: At the time, the construction of temples and places of worship was central to religious practice. People often thought that God resided in these buildings, which made Stephen's message radical.
49.interpretation: This verse teaches us that God is omnipresent and cannot be confined to a physical space. It reminds us that our relationship with Him does not depend on places of worship, but on the disposition of our hearts.
49.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on the nature of our worship and our conception of God. Rather than seeking to limit Him to a place, we must recognize that He desires to dwell within us. This encourages us to live an authentic faith, where our very lives become a meeting place with the Lord.

mots.sens: The word 'χειρ' means 'hand' in Greek. It evokes not only the physical organ but also the idea of power, action, and ability. In a theological context, the 'hand' of God symbolizes His active intervention in history and His sovereignty over creation. Thus, this term emphasizes that it is by divine power that all things have been accomplished.

The verb 'ποιέω' means 'to do' or 'to make'. It implies a creative and intentional action, often associated with the idea of God's work in the world. In this verse, it emphasizes that the visible and invisible works of God are the result of His will and sovereign power, reinforcing the idea that nothing is left to chance.

50.epoque: This verse comes from a time when the early Christians faced increasing persecution, particularly from Jewish and Roman authorities. It was a time of religious and political tensions in Palestine in the first century.
50.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, where he recalls the history of Israel and God's faithfulness to His people. Chapter 7 of the Acts of the Apostles is a powerful defense that highlights the continuity between the Old Testament and the Christian message.
50.culture: At that time, Jewish culture deeply valued history and national identity, often linked to God's work in their past. The stories of the ancestors were essential for understanding the relationship between God and His people.
50.interpretation: In this verse, Stephen emphasizes that it is the hand of God that has orchestrated all actions in history, thus affirming divine sovereignty. This reminds us that God is at work in our lives and in the world, even when we do not see it immediately.
50.commentaire: This passage encourages us to recognize the hand of God in our daily lives. By reflecting on His works, we are called to live with the confidence that God is active and present, even in difficult moments. This compels us to give glory to God for all He has accomplished and to commit ourselves to being instruments of His will on earth.

mots.sens: This term literally means 'hard of heart' and refers to an attitude of resistance and hardening in the face of divine truth. It evokes an inability to receive God's revelation, illustrating a spiritual rebellion that hinders personal transformation. In the context of this verse, it underscores the continuity of opposition to the Holy Spirit, both among the ancestors and the current generation.

This word means 'one who listens' and is often used to refer to a person attentive to the word. However, here it is used in a pejorative sense, indicating that these listeners are not receptive to divine teaching. This highlights the importance of active spiritual listening and a willingness to obey God's voice.

This term means 'holy' and refers to what is consecrated to God. In this verse, it refers to the Holy Spirit, emphasizing the divine and sacred nature of God's presence among men. Opposition to the Holy Spirit thus represents a rebellion against divine holiness and authority, with serious spiritual consequences.

This word means 'fathers' and refers to the ancestors, particularly those who preceded the current generation in faith. In the context of this verse, it highlights the continuity of disobedience to God across generations, indicating that the behaviors and attitudes of the ancestors are repeated in their descendants, calling for awareness and change.

51.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, during the early days of the Christian Church, in a context where Jewish believers faced tensions with established religious authorities.
51.passage: This passage is part of Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, who defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. He recalls the history of Israel to show how the people have often rejected God's messengers.
51.culture: At that time, circumcision was a strong symbol of Jewish identity and the covenant with God. The uncircumcision of heart and ears evokes a spiritual condition of rejection of the divine covenant and the teaching of the prophets.
51.interpretation: Stephen accuses his audience of following in the footsteps of their ancestors by opposing the Holy Spirit. This highlights the seriousness of their disobedience and warns them of the consequences of their spiritual hardening.
51.commentaire: This verse calls us to deep introspection regarding our receptivity to God's voice. As believers, we must be careful not to be 'stiff-necked' or 'uncircumcised in heart', but rather open to the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Repentance and humility are essential to receive the grace and truth that God desires to reveal to us.

mots.sens: The term 'prophet' designates a spokesperson for God, often tasked with delivering divine messages to the people. In the biblical context, prophets were often rejected and persecuted for their words that denounced injustice and announced the coming of the Messiah. The theological significance of this word underscores the continuity of God's plan throughout history, where prophets announce the coming of the Righteous One, Jesus Christ.

The word 'just' means one who is in accordance with God's will, just in actions and intentions. In this verse, it refers to Jesus, the Just One, whose life and work are the perfect model of justice. This highlights the contrast between divine justice embodied in Christ and the injustice of men who rejected Him.

This term means 'to deliver' or 'to betray', and it is often used to describe the handing over of a person to an enemy. In this context, it emphasizes the betrayal of religious leaders towards Jesus, the Just One, and highlights the gravity of their act. Spiritually, this illustrates human rebellion against God and the necessity of repentance.

52.epoque: The historical context of this passage is set in the first century, during the early days of the Christian Church, where the apostles preached the Gospel in a hostile environment, particularly facing Jewish and Roman authorities.
52.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech, the first martyr, who defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. He recalls the history of Israel and the persecution of the prophets, culminating in the accusation of the betrayal of religious leaders towards Jesus.
52.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, prophets were revered, but their message was often rejected by the authorities. This rejection is a recurring theme in Israel's history, highlighting the resistance to divine truth.
52.interpretation: This verse challenges how men react to the revealed truth of God. It highlights the human tendency to persecute those who proclaim divine will and calls for reflection on our own reception of the truth of the Gospel.
52.commentaire: This passage reminds us that faithfulness to God can lead to opposition, but we are called to remain steadfast in our faith. By recognizing Jesus as the Just One, we are invited to reflect on our own relationship with Him and not to repeat the mistake of those who rejected the Messiah. Let us be courageous witnesses of the truth, even in the face of adversity.

mots.sens: This term refers to the law, particularly the Mosaic law. It evokes the idea of a rule or standard established by God to guide His people. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the responsibility of the Israelites to obey the law they received, highlighting their failure to uphold it despite their knowledge of divine commandments.

This word means 'messenger' and is often used to refer to angels, spiritual beings sent by God. In this context, it indicates that the law was transmitted by heavenly intermediaries, thus underscoring the holiness and importance of divine law. It also reminds us that rejecting this law is a rejection of the divine authority that instituted it.

This verb means 'to keep', 'to observe', or 'to protect'. It implies a voluntary and constant action of following God's commandments. In the verse, it is used to express the failure of the listeners to respect divine precepts, which has serious implications for their relationship with God and their spiritual destiny.

53.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, at a time when Christianity was emerging within Judaism, facing tensions with Jewish religious authorities.
53.passage: Acts 7 recounts Stephen's speech, where he recalls the history of Israel and their disobedience to God, culminating in the accusation of their resistance to the Holy Spirit.
53.culture: In Jewish culture, the law was central to identity and religious practice. The commandments were not only rules but also a means of maintaining a relationship with God.
53.interpretation: This verse highlights the seriousness of disobedience to divine law. It sheds light on the individual and collective responsibility of the Israelites in light of God's revelation, and their inability to live according to His precepts.
53.commentaire: This passage reminds us that knowing God's law is not enough; it is imperative to apply it in our daily lives. As believers, we are called to live according to Christ's commandments, who has given us a new law of love. This compels us to examine our own faithfulness to God's word and to seek a life of submission and obedience.

mots.sens: This term denotes intense anger, fervent passion, or indignation. It evokes a strong emotional reaction, often associated with a desire for vengeance or justice. In this verse, it highlights the depth of the listeners' opposition to Stephen, revealing their rejection of the proclaimed truth. Spiritually, this reminds us that anger can obscure discernment and lead to destructive actions.

This word is often translated as 'to grind' or 'to rage', and it evokes an action of gnashing or grinding teeth, symbolizing a reaction of frustration or rage. In the context of this verse, it illustrates the violence of the listeners' emotions in response to the truth. This teaches us that confronting God's truth can provoke extreme reactions in those who choose to reject it.

54.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context where nascent Christianity often faced opposition from Jewish religious authorities and political leaders of the time.
54.passage: Acts 7 describes Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, who recalls the history of Israel to demonstrate God's faithfulness in the face of human unfaithfulness. Verse 54 shows the violent reaction of the listeners to the proclamation of truth.
54.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, anger and opposition were often responses to challenges to authority and tradition. The listeners' reaction underscores the tension between Jesus' teachings and established beliefs.
54.interpretation: The listeners' anger symbolizes the rejection of divine truth and resistance to the work of the Holy Spirit. This reminds us that the proclamation of the Gospel can provoke opposing reactions, ranging from acceptance to anger, depending on the state of each person's heart.
54.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on our own reaction to God's truth. Are we open to correction and teaching, or do we react with anger and resistance? As believers, we must strive to welcome the truth with humility, seeking to be transformed rather than defending ourselves. The anger that brews within us can distance us from communion with God and others.

mots.sens: This term means 'full' and evokes the idea of fullness or saturation. In the context of Stephen, it indicates that he is entirely under the influence of the Holy Spirit, which allows him to perceive spiritual reality beyond what is visible. The theological significance of this word underscores the importance of living a Spirit-filled life to have a clear vision of God's glory.

This word means 'glory' and refers to splendor, majesty, and divine recognition. In this verse, the 'glory of God' that Stephen sees testifies to the heavenly reality and divine presence. Theologically, this reminds us that God's glory is accessible to those who are in communion with Him and that this vision can transform our understanding of our faith.

This word means 'standing' and evokes a posture of authority and presence. Jesus, standing at the right hand of God, symbolizes His role as intercessor and defender of believers. This underscores the dignity and power of Christ in heaven, and reminds us that, even in our trials, we have an advocate with the Father.

This expression means 'Holy Spirit' and refers to the third person of the Trinity. The Holy Spirit is the one who guides, teaches, and fills believers with the presence of God. In this verse, the fact that Stephen is filled with the Holy Spirit highlights the necessity of spiritual dependence to discern divine truth and live an authentic Christian life.

55.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context of persecution of early Christians, where faith in Christ was often tested by Jewish and Roman authorities.
55.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen, the first Christian martyr, defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. This chapter highlights his courageous testimony and heavenly vision before his martyrdom, underscoring the power of the Holy Spirit in moments of crisis.
55.culture: At this time, Jewish culture was deeply rooted in tradition and law, and believers in Christ were often seen as heretics. Stephen's vision of God's glory and Jesus standing at His right hand challenges this culture by affirming the reality of the risen Christ.
55.interpretation: Stephen's vision is an affirmation of God's sovereignty and Jesus' place of honor in heaven. This reminds us that, even in moments of opposition, God is present and active, and that our faith can give us an eternal perspective on our trials.
55.commentaire: This verse encourages us to seek a life filled with the Holy Spirit, so that we can discern God's glory in our lives. Like Stephen, we are called to testify to our faith with courage, knowing that we have an advocate with God. In our struggles, may we fix our eyes on God's glory and the promise of His presence with us.

mots.sens: This expression literally means 'Son of Man'. It is used by Jesus to refer to both His humanity and His divinity. As the Son of Man, Jesus fully identifies with humanity while affirming His divine authority. In this verse, Stephen's vision highlights the dignity and majesty of Christ, who, although being a man, is also the sovereign at the right hand of God.

The word 'ouranos' means 'heavens' and refers not only to the physical sky but also to the spiritual realm where God reigns. In the biblical context, the heavens are often associated with the divine presence and revelation of God. Stephen's vision of the opened heavens indicates a divine revelation and direct access to the majesty of God.

The term 'hestota' means 'standing' and evokes a posture of dignity, authority, and intercession. In the context of this verse, it shows that Jesus is not only seated but stands to welcome Stephen, thus emphasizing His active role as a mediator between God and humanity. This reinforces the idea that Christ is alive and engaged in the affairs of His people.

56.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the early days of the Christian Church, at a time when believers faced increasing persecution.
56.passage: In Acts 7, Stephen, the first Christian martyr, defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. His speech recalls the history of Israel and culminates in his vision of Jesus, which provokes his arrest and stoning.
56.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued visions and divine revelations. The opened heavens were a powerful symbol of divine approval and spiritual revelation.
56.interpretation: Stephen's vision is a powerful testimony to the reality of the risen Christ. It shows that even in suffering and death, believers can have the assurance of God's presence and Jesus' intercession on their behalf.
56.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even in the most difficult moments, we have a Savior who stands at the right hand of God, ready to intercede for us. Like Stephen, we are called to remain faithful in our testimony, knowing that our faith in Christ opens the heavens and assures us of His constant presence.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to cry out' or 'to shout', and it evokes an intense expression of emotion or despair. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the violent opposition and anger of the listeners in response to the truth proclaimed by Stephen. Spiritually, this cry can symbolize the rejection of God's word and the hardening of hearts against divine revelation.

This word means 'to seal' or 'to close' and is often used to denote the action of sealing something. Here, it illustrates the attitude of the listeners who, by stopping their ears, deliberately choose to ignore the truth. This underscores the theological significance of resisting the Holy Spirit and the importance of attentive listening to God's word.

This verb means 'to rush upon' or 'to fall upon', indicating a violent and collective action. In this verse, it shows the unity of the opponents in their rejection of the truth. Spiritually, this highlights the nature of the conflict between the light of the Gospel and the darkness of unbelief.

57.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the early days of the Christian Church, in a context of increasing tensions between believers and Jewish authorities. The early Christians faced persecution because of their faith in Jesus Christ.
57.passage: This verse is part of Stephen's speech, the first Christian martyr, who defends his faith before the Sanhedrin. His message, which emphasizes the history of the people of Israel and their rebellion against God, provokes a violent reaction from his listeners.
57.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, honor and shame played a central role, and public disapproval could lead to extreme reactions. The cries and physical aggression reflect a loss of control in the face of a message that challenges their beliefs and authority.
57.interpretation: This verse illustrates the rejection of divine truth and how hardened hearts can react to the proclamation of the Gospel. The listeners' reaction shows that the truth can provoke violent responses from those who choose not to accept it.
57.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of listening attentively to God's word and not stopping our ears to the truth. As believers, we must be aware of the resistances we may encounter in our testimony and pray for receptive hearts, both for ourselves and for those who hear the message of the Gospel.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to stone' and evokes the action of killing by throwing stones. In the biblical context, this represents a form of public and brutal punishment, often associated with accusations of blasphemy or unfaithfulness to God's law. Spiritually, the stoning of Stephen symbolizes the resistance to divine truth and the persecution of witnesses for Christ, thus highlighting the tensions between the world and the Church.

This term means 'witness' and is the root of the word 'martyr'. It designates someone who testifies to the truth, often at the cost of their life. In this verse, the witnesses of Stephen's stoning are representatives of the law, but their act testifies to their rejection of divine revelation in Christ, illustrating the cost of testimony for faith.

This name refers to Saul of Tarsus, who will become the Apostle Paul. His presence in this verse highlights the beginning of his journey that will lead to his conversion. Saul, as a young man, represents misdirected religious fervor and opposition to the Gospel, but also the hope of redemption and transformation that God can bring to those who persecute His Church.

This verb means 'to drag out' and implies a forced action. In this context, it symbolizes the rejection and exclusion of Stephen from the community. Spiritually, this represents how the message of the Gospel is often rejected by those who are attached to their traditions and comfort, illustrating the cost of faithfulness to Christ.

58.epoque: This passage is set at the beginning of the Christian Church, in a context where believers are often persecuted for their faith, particularly by the Jewish authorities of the time.
58.passage: This verse is part of the account of the first martyrdom of the Church, where Stephen, a deacon, is stoned for his bold testimony about Jesus Christ. This chapter highlights the resistance of religious leaders to the proclamation of the Gospel.
58.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, stoning was a legal method of execution for serious crimes, including blasphemy. This shows the intolerance towards those who questioned traditional teachings.
58.interpretation: The fact that the witnesses lay their garments at Saul's feet symbolizes a tacit approval of the violence and involvement in the act of persecution. It also highlights Saul's future transformation, as he will become a fervent defender of the faith he once persecuted.
58.commentaire: This verse reminds us that faithfulness to Christ can lead to suffering and persecution. However, it encourages us to remain steadfast in our testimony, even in the face of opposition, for God can transform those who seem to be His enemies into powerful instruments of His Gospel. The life of Stephen and the future conversion of Saul remind us that God's grace is capable of touching even the hardest of hearts.

mots.sens: This word means 'breath' or 'spirit'. In the context of this verse, it refers to the human spirit that is entrusted to God. The root of the word evokes the notion of life and vitality, emphasizing the intimate relationship between man and the divine. Theologically, this reminds us that the spirit of man belongs to God and must be returned to Him, which is particularly poignant in the context of martyrdom.

This term means 'Lord' and is used to designate a supreme authority. In this verse, Stephen addresses Jesus as Lord, thus affirming His divinity and central role in salvation. This word also emphasizes the individual's submission to divine will, which is crucial in the Christian life, especially in times of suffering and persecution.

This verb means 'to give back' or 'to return'. In the context of Stephen's prayer, it evokes the act of surrendering his spirit to God. This notion of restitution highlights Stephen's trust in divine providence, even in the face of death, and sheds light on the dependent relationship between the believer and God.

59.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, during the early days of the Christian Church, a period marked by the persecution of believers and the proclamation of the Gospel in a hostile Jewish and Roman context.
59.passage: Acts 7 describes Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin, where he recalls the history of Israel and accuses the religious leaders of their resistance to God. This chapter culminates in his martyrdom, illustrating the tension between the nascent Christian faith and established authorities.
59.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, stoning was a form of capital punishment for serious crimes, including blasphemy. Stephen, as a deacon and witness of Christ, embodies faith unto death, defying the cultural and religious norms of his time.
59.interpretation: Stephen's prayer, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit', is an act of faith and trust in Jesus even in ultimate suffering. It underscores the continuity between the death of Jesus and that of His disciples, showing that faith in Christ transcends death.
59.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of prayer in times of crisis. Like Stephen, we are called to entrust our spirit into God's hands, even in trials. It teaches us to live our faith with courage and to testify to Christ's love, even in the face of opposition.

mots.sens: This word means 'Lord' and is used to designate a higher authority. It evokes not only God's sovereignty but also a personal relationship with Him. In this verse, Stephen's use of 'Lord' emphasizes his faith and total dependence on God, even in moments of suffering, and shows the depth of his spiritual commitment.

This verb means 'to forgive' or 'to let go'. It refers to the idea of releasing someone from an obligation or debt, and in the spiritual context, it implies grace and mercy. By asking God not to hold this sin against them, Stephen demonstrates a heart full of forgiveness, reflecting the character of Christ who also prayed for His executioners.

This term means 'to fall asleep' and is often used in the New Testament to describe the death of believers. It carries a connotation of peace and rest, suggesting that death for a Christian is not an end, but a passage to eternal life. In this verse, it underscores Stephen's faith in the resurrection and the promise of eternal life.

60.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, at a time when the nascent Christian Church faced strong opposition and persecution, particularly from Jewish authorities.
60.passage: This verse concludes the account of Stephen's martyrdom, the first Christian martyr, in chapter 7 of the Acts of the Apostles. It illustrates Stephen's courage and faith as he is stoned for his proclamation of the Gospel.
60.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, forgiveness was a complex concept, often linked to divine justice. By asking for forgiveness for his executioners, Stephen challenges the cultural norms of vengeance and retribution.
60.interpretation: This verse highlights the spirit of forgiveness and grace, even in the darkest moments. Stephen's prayer for his persecutors is a model of how Christians are called to respond to injustice with love and mercy, following the example of Christ.
60.commentaire: Stephen's cry on his knees reminds us of the importance of prayer in times of suffering. His example encourages us to adopt an attitude of forgiveness towards those who wrong us, thus reflecting God's unconditional love. As believers, we are called to live our faith with courage, even in the face of adversity, keeping our eyes fixed on the promise of eternal life.
